stories.title: Introducing the pkg.go.dev API
stories.snippet: The Go Blog Introducing the pkg.go.dev API Ethan Lee, Hana Kim, and Jonathan Amsterdam 21 May 2026 Since its inception, pkg.go.dev has established itself as the Go community’s primary resource for package documentation and discovery. While we initially prioritized creating a comprehensive and highly accessible web interface for users, the need for programmatic access has become increasingly
stories.summary: The Go team has launched the official pkg.go.dev API, providing programmatic access to metadata about published Go modules and replacing the need for fragile web scraping. Built for stability and efficient caching, the stateless GET-only API is currently hosted under the /v1beta path, with plans to transition to a formal v1 release following community feedback. Core endpoints cover packages, modules, versions, search, symbols, imported-by relationships, and vulnerabilities. A key design principle is precision over convenience, requiring clients to specify the module explicitly when package paths are ambiguous, unlike the web interface which automatically applies the longest module path rule. The API supports a version query parameter for specific semantic versions or master/main branches, defaulting to the latest tagged version when omitted. To demonstrate usage, the team released pkgsite-cli, a reference command-line client that handles pagination and formatting, while committing to backward compatibility as the interface evolves.

stories.title: Type Construction and Cycle Detection
stories.snippet: The Go Blog Type Construction and Cycle Detection Mark Freeman 24 March 2026 Go’s static typing is an important part of why Go is a good fit for production systems that have to be robust and reliable. When a Go package is compiled, it is first parsed—meaning that the Go source code within that package is converted into an abstract syntax tree (or AST). This AST is then passed to the Go type
stories.summary: Go's type checker constructs internal representations for each type it encounters while traversing the abstract syntax tree, a process called type construction. Types begin as "under construction" and only become "complete" once all their dependencies are fully populated. Recursive types complicate this process, since evaluating a type expression may return an incomplete type rather than a complete one, making deconstruction unsound until construction finishes. While type construction can safely refer to incomplete types, operations like unsafe.Sizeof require deconstruction, which can create cycles. For example, type T [unsafe.Sizeof(T{})]int is invalid because calculating the array's size requires deconstruction of T, which cannot complete until the array completes, making the cycle impossible to satisfy. Go 1.26 significantly improved the type checker's handling of these cycle errors, reducing corner cases without producing observable changes for typical Go users.

stories.title: //go:fix inline and the source-level inliner
stories.snippet: The Go Blog //go:fix inline and the source-level inliner Alan Donovan 10 March 2026 .beforeafter { justify-content: center; display: grid; gap: 1em; margin: 1em; grid-template-columns: minmax(min-content, 1fr) auto minmax(min-content, 1fr); font-size: 180%; @media screen and (max-width: 57.7rem) { grid-template-columns: 1fr; } } #content .beforeafter pre { margin: 0em; /* Handled by grid gap */ }
stories.summary: Go 1.26 introduces an updated `go fix` command featuring a source-level inliner that replaces function calls with copies of the callee's body, substituting arguments for parameters. Unlike compiler inlining that operates on ephemeral intermediate representations, source-level inlining durably modifies source code and is used by gopls for refactorings like "Change signature" and "Remove unused parameter." A new `//go:fix inline` directive allows package authors to mark deprecated functions for automatic migration, enabling self-service API updates such as replacing `ioutil.ReadFile` with `os.ReadFile` or correcting design flaws like swapped parameter orders. The directive works on types and constants as well, and at Google it has already prepared more than 18,000 changelists in the monorepo. Implementing the inliner required about 7,000 lines of compiler-like logic to handle complex edge cases, including parameter elimination when arguments are trivial literals.

stories.title: Enabling the next iteration of the borrow checker on nightly
stories.snippet: TL;DR We are enabling the next iteration of the borrow checker (coined Polonius Alpha) on nightly in preparation for stabilization in the next few months. Whaaaaaat? Yes! You heard it right! The next iteration of the Rust borrow checker is coming! Rust's first borrow checker ("AST borrowck") was very limited and was phased out in 2019 in favor of NLL, other than a "migrate mode" that was used to p
stories.summary: The next iteration of Rust's borrow checker, dubbed Polonius Alpha, is being enabled on nightly for testing before stabilization later this year. Its key advantage over the current NLL borrow checker is flow-sensitive analysis of lifetime outlives relationships, which allows code patterns like the `reborrow` and `get_mut_or_default` examples to compile. Polonius Alpha is not a full superset of the original legacy Polonius, as some programs accepted by legacy Polonius are rejected by Polonius Alpha. Performance is generally acceptable for stabilization, with relatively few significant regressions among the top 10,000 crates on crates.io, and a worst case of roughly 2-3x slowdown. Users can disable it via `-Zpolonius=off` if needed, and the team plans to monitor for issues, address performance regressions, and stabilize before year's end. After stabilization, no concrete plans exist for further Polonius feature work, though optimization will continue and future feature work may resume eventually.

stories.title: Announcing Rust 1.97.1
stories.snippet: The Rust team has published a new point release of Rust, 1.97.1. Rust is a programming language that is empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software. If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, getting Rust 1.97.1 is as easy as: rustup update stable If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website. What's in 1.97.1 Rust 1.97
stories.summary: The Rust team has released version 1.97.1 of Rust, a programming language empowering developers to build reliable and efficient software. Users with a previous version installed via rustup can update by running "rustup update stable." This point release fixes a miscompilation in an LLVM optimization by backporting an LLVM fix and disabling a change introduced in Rust 1.97.0 that affected Rust's generated IR. The Rust team noted that the underlying miscompilation had been present since at least Rust 1.87. Developers can help test future releases by running their code's CI or local builds on the beta or nightly channels and reporting any bugs they encounter. The team thanked all contributors for making this release possible.

stories.title: Surgical WAM: A World-Action Model for Data-Efficient Surgical Robot Learning
stories.summary: Learning reliable surgical manipulation policies is limited by the scarcity of costly action-labeled teleoperated demonstrations, while endoscopic video is comparatively inexpensive and abundant. Existing surgical world models rarely translate learned visual dynamics into closed-loop control, leaving open whether action-free video pretraining can improve closed-loop manipulation under a fixed action budget. To address this, the authors introduce the Surgical World-Action Model (Surgical WAM), a unified generative model built on Cosmos Policy that jointly predicts future endoscopic observations and executable surgical robot action chunks. The model first learns surgical visual dynamics from action-free video, is fine-tuned on a limited action-labeled budget, and acts at deployment as a receding-horizon controller that replans from each new observation. On four simulated surgical manipulation tasks, video pretraining raised the average success rate from 63.5% to 77.8%, including a 20-percentage-point gain on PegTransfer, with the largest improvements on contact-rich and bimanual tasks.

stories.title: ConVAWG: A Retrieval-Grounded Framework for Controlled Synthetic Dialogue Generation in Violence Against Women and Girls
stories.summary: ConVAWG is a retrieval-grounded framework introduced by Chen Lyu and colleagues for generating synthetic multi-turn dialogues depicting Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG) scenarios. The work addresses privacy and legal barriers that limit access to real conversation data and the gap in modeling abuse as a relational, temporally unfolding phenomenon rather than sentence-level toxicity. ConVAWG constructs scenarios from persona seeds, demographic patterns from the UK Office for National Statistics, official crime definitions, and retrieved Domestic Homicide Review cases, then converts them into hierarchical event timelines for multi-scene role-play generation. Targeted activation-steered toxicity control is applied to appropriate utterances during generation. The authors released over 6,000 multi-turn dialogue events across 200 scenarios with rich metadata at scenario, event, and turn levels. Evaluation through human assessment, LLM-as-Judge, ablations, and downstream tasks demonstrates strong dialogue quality and domain fidelity.

stories.title: Long-Horizon AI Research for Grothendieck Constant: A Case Study in Human-AI Mathematical Collaboration
stories.summary: Researchers Alan Li, Rahul Saha, Anton Xue, Swarat Chaudhuri, Adam Klivans, Pravesh K Kothari, and Raghu Meka present an extensive case study exploring how AI can be effectively used in mathematics research, focused on improving bounds for the Grothendieck constant KG. The Grothendieck constant captures the hardness gap between combinatorial problems and their continuous relaxations, though its precise value remains unknown. Using an AI research system, the team tightened the best known bounds to 6π/11 ≤ KG ≤ π/(2log(1+√2)) − 10⁻⁴. The improvements were achieved through insights that domain experts deemed novel. The authors detail their experience using AI for mathematical research, discussing both its strengths and weaknesses, along with conditions that enable AI systems to arrive at breakthrough insights during long-horizon research tasks.

stories.title: How to Verify Consistency of Probabilistic Claims
stories.summary: The paper "How to Verify Consistency of Probabilistic Claims" by Orr Paradise, Oliver Richardson, Yoshua Bengio, and Shafi Goldwasser addresses whether a probabilistic predictor's many conditional-probability answers are self-consistent and whether this can be verified in polynomial time, a question relevant to AI safety. The authors construct an interactive PCP in which a polynomial-time verifier, given a probability circuit P and a confidence circuit Q that together specify exponentially many probabilistic claims, evaluates them at only a few points. Alongside the circuits, a proof oracle encodes an alleged witnessing probability distribution, which the verifier reads at few locations while interacting with a single untrusted prover. The work first handles explicit probabilistic claims—m claims of the form Pr[Y=1|X=x]=p over n Boolean variables—placing l_2-approximate probabilistic consistency in NP with certificates of length O(mn + log B) in input bit-precision B, building on Nilsson's 1986 work. A small additive completeness-soundness gap removes the dependence on B, and together these results provide a complexity-theoretic foundation for certifying self-consistency of probabilistic predictors.

stories.title: Npm-scan: Modern supply chain security for the npm ecosystem
stories.snippet: Npm-scan: Modern supply chain security for the npm ecosystem
stories.summary: npm-scan is a supply chain security tool designed for the npm ecosystem, distributed as the @lateos/npm-scan package on npm and licensed under MIT or BLA. The project claims to detect threats that existing tools like npm audit, Snyk, and Socket miss, specifically targeting obfuscated payloads, credential stealers, kernel rootkits, eBPF hooks, memory extraction, GitHub spoofing, and AI-targeted attacks. Its repository hosts a backend, CLI, API, helm deployment charts, Docker configurations, and documentation in multiple languages including German, French, Hebrew, Japanese, and Chinese. The codebase includes 830+ passing tests, capture-the-flag campaign fixtures, validation reports, and detection rate metrics. Additional features include a GitHub Action and files for verifying production readiness and phase-based release management.

stories.title: Show HN: Open-Source Greptile Alternative
stories.summary: Juror-AI/juror is an open-source GitHub-based code review tool that uses frontier AI models to review pull requests in parallel, positioning itself as a self-hostable alternative to Greptile. It is distributed as a GitHub Action (juror-ai), runs on Node ≥20, and is MIT-licensed, with the project dogfooding itself by using Juror to review its own code. The repository includes source code, tests, documentation, scripts, and a bundled benchmark corpus. According to the project's README, on a manually adjudicated production-PR seed, Juror Fast reportedly identified 4 of 6 P0–P2 defects with 100% precision, compared to Greptile's 1 of 6 at 50% precision. However, the authors explicitly note this is a one-PR seed rather than a statistically sufficient benchmark, and invite users to inspect the corpus, methodology, and reproduce the results themselves.

stories.title: How Tailscale helped find the SQLite WAL-Reset bug
stories.snippet: Previously, the SQLite release fixing this bug. Comments
stories.summary: Tailscale's control plane uses SQLite databases to manage tailnet configurations. Beginning in August, they encountered 19 separate instances of database corruption over six months, each requiring the control plane process to be stopped for repairs and causing downtime for affected tailnets. They engaged the SQLite developers through a professional support contract and built a transaction logging pipeline that enabled database restoration without data loss. This pipeline unexpectedly revealed that data committed by one transaction was mysteriously invisible to later transactions. Working with the SQLite developers and their new debugging tool, which provided better visibility into the WAL checkpoint process, they ultimately tracked down a long-standing bug in SQLite.

stories.title: DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813
stories.summary: DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 is a large-scale mixture-of-experts model from DeepSeek, representing the GA release of DeepSeek V4 Pro. It is a text-in, text-out model with a context window of 1,048,576 tokens, released on August 12, 2026. Pricing is set at $0.435 per million input tokens and $0.87 per million output tokens, with cache reads available at $0.003625 per million tokens. On OpenRouter, the model is hosted by a single provider, with requests forwarded directly rather than routed. The page also tracks throughput, latency, time-to-first-token, uptime, and benchmark scores to help users evaluate the model's performance alongside real-world activity from public apps.

stories.title: AI is removing the middle class of software engineering?
stories.snippet: AI is removing the middle class of software engineering?
stories.summary: AI has made software implementation dramatically cheaper, allowing anyone to generate thousands of lines of code in an afternoon. However, this speed causes projects with weak engineering cultures to fail faster, as bad decisions compound before anyone can properly review or understand them. Reverting poor decisions is extremely difficult because of database migrations, foreign keys, and the risk of disrupting live systems. As a result, companies increasingly value engineers with strong judgment who can evaluate AI recommendations, question unnecessary abstractions, and understand how systems actually work. The article predicts AI will push engineering salaries further apart, making top engineers more valuable while bad engineers become cheaper to hire or get replaced entirely. The same dynamic is likely to play out across most knowledge work, where AI amplifies the productivity of skilled professionals while making incompetent ones nearly unemployable.

stories.title: I hate packaging my software for Linux
stories.summary: The author describes frustrations with packaging their software, Fresh, for Linux due to the variety of distributions and packaging formats. While Windows and macOS are relatively uniform and easier to support, Linux required creating packages across numerous channels including npm, cargo, AppImage, Flatpak, deb, rpm, AUR, nix, mise, homebrew for Linux, and Terra Gentoo, each with their own drawbacks. Issues include AppImage's slow startup requiring FUSE, Flatpak's sandboxing being unsuitable for a terminal TUI, Debian requiring all Rust dependencies to be packaged separately, and lack of automatic updates without official source acceptance. The Arch AUR has also been in read-only mode due to security breaches, causing missed releases. Going forward, the author plans to focus on a statically linked musl binary with built-in self-updating capabilities as the main Linux release channel.
